content.text:
Short answer up front
- The most robust, user-friendly, and future‑proof approach in today’s MCP ecosystem is to register six separate tools (memory.view, memory.create, memory.str_replace, memory.insert, memory.delete, memory.rename) rather than one discriminated‑union “memory” tool. This matches real‑world servers, works across clients (Claude Code, Cursor, MCP Inspector), avoids current JSON Schema/union quirks in clients, and gives clearer ergonomics to the LLM and the UI. ([flowhunt.io](https://www.flowhunt.io/mcp-servers/golang-filesystem-server/?utm_source=openai))
- If you insist on a single tool, the safest pattern under the current TypeScript SDK (v1.x) is Option 2 (nest the discriminated union under a property like params). It preserves TypeScript type narrowing while avoiding top‑level oneOf/anyOf that some tooling and registries still choke on. ([modelcontextprotocol.io](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/server/tools))
- I do not recommend Option 3 (manually overriding the SDK’s inputSchema) because it is fragile against SDK updates and can introduce top‑level union shapes that some clients/registries reject today. ([glama.ai](https://glama.ai/mcp/servers/%40kesslerio/attio-mcp-server/blob/f3302a945c812139d2cc3b26bfefac5c74b75ca0/docs/mcp-schema-guidelines.md?utm_source=openai))

Below is a complete analysis with sources, trade‑offs, DX and type‑safety notes, and recommendations.

What the spec and SDK officially support today
- Tools accept a JSON Schema inputSchema; the spec’s examples show a simple object with properties and required. The spec does not prescribe your exact shape beyond “JSON Schema,” but most examples keep it to “type: object” with flat properties. ([modelcontextprotocol.io](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/server/tools))
- The official TypeScript SDK encourages passing a Zod raw shape (object of fields) which it wraps with z.object() to generate JSON Schema. The readme examples reflect this (“inputSchema: { a: z.number(), b: z.number() }”). ([github.com](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk))
- There is an open PR to allow passing a full ZodType<object> (including unions) directly to registerTool, but as of October 2025 this PR is not merged, so you can’t rely on it for production. If/when merged, you could pass a discriminated union directly (still subject to client compatibility). ([github.com](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk/issues/816))
- The MCP project is clarifying JSON Schema dialect expectations and composition support (anyOf/oneOf). A spec proposal points toward standardizing on JSON Schema 2020‑12 and allowing compositions like anyOf/oneOf, but real clients vary in how well they handle unions. Plan for conservative schemas when targeting multiple clients. ([github.com](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol/issues/834?utm_source=openai))

Client reality: unions and complex schemas are still bumpy
- Multiple reports indicate some MCP clients (notably certain Claude Code/Desktop builds) struggle with complex parameter schemas (e.g., JSON objects passed as strings, unions misunderstood, required fields guessed). This pushes server authors toward simple, single‑responsibility tool shapes. ([github.com](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/5504?utm_source=openai))
- A widely circulated guideline (non‑official but aligned with observed behavior) warns against top‑level oneOf/allOf/anyOf in inputSchema; instead, keep top‑level as an object and perform either/or validation in code or nest unions below the top level. Even where the protocol allows it, some registries/clients/validators still fail on top‑level compositions. ([glama.ai](https://glama.ai/mcp/servers/%40kesslerio/attio-mcp-server/blob/f3302a945c812139d2cc3b26bfefac5c74b75ca0/docs/mcp-schema-guidelines.md?utm_source=openai))

How practitioners structure tools
- Production MCP servers for filesystem operations overwhelmingly use separate tools per action (read_file, write_file, move_file, delete_file, etc.). This avoids the “one tool with a command discriminator” pattern and gives the LLM and UI a clearer menu of affordances. It also prevents accidental parameter mixing across actions. ([flowhunt.io](https://www.flowhunt.io/mcp-servers/golang-filesystem-server/?utm_source=openai))

Your three options, deeply analyzed

Option 1: Flat schema with all optional fields (current)
- What it looks like: One tool with a command enum and many optional parameters, and you validate at runtime after switching on command.
- Pros
  - Satisfies the SDK’s ZodRawShape constraint without hacks.
  - Flat API surface from the client’s perspective.
- Cons
  - You lose compile‑time inference at the tool boundary; everything is optional and you only recover types after manual validation. The callback signature sees a lax type, making refactors dangerous.
  - It communicates to clients/LLMs that every field is optional, which increases bad calls, retries, and tool misuse (poorer DX for humans in UIs as well).
- When to consider: If you must keep a single tool name for backwards compatibility, you can mitigate by immediately parsing the input with a discriminated union inside the callback:
  - const parsed = MemoryCommands.parse(input); switch (parsed.command) { … }
  This recovers type narrowing, but only inside the callback; it doesn’t improve the published JSON Schema (the client still sees many optional fields).

Option 2: Nest the discriminated union under params (recommended if you insist on one tool)
- What it looks like: inputSchema: { params: z.discriminatedUnion('command', [...]) } and then handle params in the callback.
- Pros
  - Excellent TypeScript narrowing in your implementation: z.infer<typeof MemoryCommands> on params gives exact types per command branch.
  - Avoids top‑level oneOf/anyOf. The top level remains a plain object, which is the most compatible shape across clients/registries today. ([glama.ai](https://glama.ai/mcp/servers/%40kesslerio/attio-mcp-server/blob/f3302a945c812139d2cc3b26bfefac5c74b75ca0/docs/mcp-schema-guidelines.md?utm_source=openai))
  - You keep a single tool “memory,” satisfying your “flat” name preference as far as tool listing goes.
- Cons
  - Callers must send { params: { command: "...", ... } }, which is one level of nesting.
  - Depending on how the client renders parameter forms, the extra nesting can be slightly more cumbersome to fill.
- Notes
  - This pattern maps cleanly to JSON Schema as an object with a property whose schema is a union, avoiding the specific pain point of top‑level compositions. It also aligns with the spec’s general examples of object‑typed inputSchema. ([modelcontextprotocol.io](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/server/tools))
  - If you later move to an SDK that accepts full ZodType<object> (PR #816), you could consider lifting the discriminated union to the top level. But test against your target clients first. ([github.com](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk/issues/816))

Option 3: Manual override of inputSchema to a discriminated union (bypass SDK)
- What it looks like: Register with an empty shape, then patch tool.inputSchema to a ZodDiscriminatedUnion yourself.
- Pros
  - Keeps your tool flat (no params wrapper) and advertises the correct union at the top level.
- Cons
  - Fragile: relies on private/internal SDK behavior and may break across versions.
  - Risk of generating a top‑level oneOf/anyOf that some discovery services or clients reject, even if the protocol technically allows it. This can cause connection/listing failures. ([glama.ai](https://glama.ai/mcp/servers/%40kesslerio/attio-mcp-server/blob/f3302a945c812139d2cc3b26bfefac5c74b75ca0/docs/mcp-schema-guidelines.md?utm_source=openai))
  - You lose type safety at the registerTool boundary and make upgrades harder.
- Verdict: Not recommended.

A fourth option you should seriously consider: register six separate tools
- What it looks like: memory.view, memory.create, memory.str_replace, memory.insert, memory.delete, memory.rename.
- Why it’s the practical standard
  - Mirrors real‑world servers (especially filesystem‑like operations) that expose one tool per action. These servers work across Claude Code, MCP Inspector, Cursor, etc. with fewer surprises. ([flowhunt.io](https://www.flowhunt.io/mcp-servers/golang-filesystem-server/?utm_source=openai))
  - Simpler schemas are easier for LLMs to select correctly. Clear names and minimal required parameters reduce retries, wasted tokens, and model confusion.
  - Better UI/UX: clients can show six obvious buttons/commands; humans can auto‑approve non‑destructive tools and scrutinize destructive ones.
  - Avoids all union/discriminator schema ambiguity outright.
- DX/type‑safety
  - Each tool’s callback parameter is precisely typed; you don’t need discriminated unions or nested params at all.
  - Easier to evolve: adding a new operation doesn’t change a central union and risk breaking prior calls—just register a new tool.

Will clients handle anyOf/oneOf properly?
- Officially, the spec says inputSchema is JSON Schema and shows object examples; it doesn’t forbid schema composition. In practice, support varies: some clients mangle complex params (e.g., serializing objects as strings), others ignore or misread unions, especially at the top level. That’s why many production servers avoid top‑level oneOf/anyOf and/or avoid unions entirely. ([modelcontextprotocol.io](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/server/tools))
- If you must use a union today, prefer nesting it (Option 2) and test with the clients you target (Claude Code, MCP Inspector, Cursor). Keep the top level as a plain object. ([glama.ai](https://glama.ai/mcp/servers/%40kesslerio/attio-mcp-server/blob/f3302a945c812139d2cc3b26bfefac5c74b75ca0/docs/mcp-schema-guidelines.md?utm_source=openai))

Official and ecosystem guidance (what we can point to)
- The Tools spec gives object‑shaped examples and emphasizes JSON Schema for parameters; it does not recommend a particular API layout beyond that. ([modelcontextprotocol.io](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/server/tools))
- The TypeScript SDK readme and examples consistently use object shapes with explicit properties—no top‑level unions. ([github.com](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk))
- There’s ongoing work to improve schema expressiveness in the SDK (accept full ZodType<object>) and to clarify JSON Schema dialect/composition in the spec, but you can’t count on uniform client behavior yet. ([github.com](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk/issues/816))
- Several community servers and directories explicitly recommend avoiding top‑level oneOf/anyOf due to client and registry validation behavior; even if not “official,” this reflects the current reality users hit. ([glama.ai](https://glama.ai/mcp/servers/%40kesslerio/attio-mcp-server/blob/f3302a945c812139d2cc3b26bfefac5c74b75ca0/docs/mcp-schema-guidelines.md?utm_source=openai))

Answering your specific questions

1) What’s standard/recommended in MCP for varying parameters?
- De facto practice is “one tool per action,” especially for CRUD‑/filesystem‑style servers, not a single discriminated‑union tool. This aligns with client UX and LLM behavior, and minimizes schema pitfalls. ([flowhunt.io](https://www.flowhunt.io/mcp-servers/golang-filesystem-server/?utm_source=openai))

2) Can you keep a flat API (no params wrapper) and maintain type safety?
- Not reliably with @modelcontextprotocol/sdk v1.0.4. You can recover type safety inside the callback by parsing the received input with your discriminated union, but compile‑time inference at registerTool’s boundary will still see the flat optional bag. If the pending PR merges in a future SDK release, you could pass a Zod discriminated union directly; just validate client compatibility (top‑level union). ([github.com](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk/issues/816))

3) Does the protocol have guidance on discriminated unions? Will clients like Claude Code handle anyOf for this?
- The protocol treats inputSchema as JSON Schema; no special MCP‑level rules for discriminated unions. However, client support for union compositions is inconsistent today; some issues show parameter serialization bugs and poor handling of complex schemas. Favor simpler object shapes; if you must use a union, nest it. ([modelcontextprotocol.io](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/server/tools))

4) Alternatives or modern patterns?
- Six separate tools (memory.view etc.) is the most interoperable pattern.
- If you want to preserve the single “memory” entry point for humans but keep technical clarity: register a lightweight “memory.help” tool that returns examples and guidance, and register the six action tools for actual work.
- If you insist on one tool for routing: Option 2 with params is the safest. Avoid Option 3 (manual override).
- If schema heaviness is a concern in Claude Code (tools bloating the context), consider grouping tools or dynamically enabling toolsets (some clients are adding features here). ([reddit.com](https://www.reddit.com/r/ClaudeAI/comments/1krvdif?utm_source=openai))

5) What’s most maintainable and user‑friendly long‑term?
- Separate tools win on maintainability, testability, and cross‑client reliability. They make it easier to:
  - add/remove operations without risking a central union schema,
  - write focused unit tests per operation,
  - provide per‑tool annotations (e.g., destructiveHint) and titles/descriptions that help both LLMs and users choose the right tool,
  - gate/auto‑approve only non‑destructive tools in client UIs.

Recommended design for your case

Preferred (separate tools)
- memory.view: { path: string, view_range?: [number, number] }
- memory.create: { path: string, file_text: string }
- memory.str_replace: { path: string, old_str: string, new_str: string }
- memory.insert: { path: string, insert_line: number, insert_text: string }
- memory.delete: { path: string }
- memory.rename: { old_path: string, new_path: string }
Rationale: clean schemas, perfect type inference, great client compatibility (no unions), nice affordances for the LLM and UI. ([flowhunt.io](https://www.flowhunt.io/mcp-servers/golang-filesystem-server/?utm_source=openai))

If you must keep one tool (use Option 2)
- Define MemoryCommands = z.discriminatedUnion('command', [...]).
- Register inputSchema: { params: MemoryCommands }.
- In the callback: const { command } = MemoryCommands.parse(params); switch (command) { … }.
- Document clearly in the tool description how to call each sub‑command; unions still need clear English guidance for LLMs.

A few TypeScript/Zod tips to keep DX high
- Strongly type your handler with z.infer<typeof MemoryCommands> to get exhaustiveness checking in the switch:
  - type MemoryParams = z.infer<typeof MemoryCommands>;
  - function handle(params: MemoryParams) { switch(params.command) { case 'view': return handleView(params); … default: assertNever(params); } }
